subject: policies/simplicity-policy.json
scenario: The failure mode of a simplicity rule is that it becomes a ban list. A policy that forbids queues blocks the project that needs one, and the organization routes around it. This case tries to make the control itself the defect: it passes only while the policy encourages and evaluates rather than prohibits.
expected_behaviors: The policy names no forbidden technology, pattern or component.
The policy states in its own text that a justified introduction is a legitimate engineering decision.
The policy states that it is not enforced by a hook, and why a hook could not tell a justified queue from an unjustified one.
The policy states that simplicity never justifies dropping a stated non-functional, reliability or security requirement.
failure_conditions: The policy prohibits a named technology or pattern outright.
The principle is stated as 'choose the smallest solution', which licenses dropping requirements.
A hook is wired to block a design or a dependency on simplicity grounds.

checks.description: No ban list of any kind.

checks.value: Not 'always choose the smallest solution'. A design that drops a stated requirement is incomplete, not simple.
checks.description: The abuse the principle is most often used for is ruled out in the policy itself.
The non-prohibition is a stated commitment, not an accident of drafting.
The limit of the mechanism is written down where the mechanism is.
No guard blocks a tool call on simplicity grounds. The control is a review dimension and a predicate.
No hook script decides on the simplicity policy, and the policy claims no enforcement it does not have.
